passages.text: On the fourth day in Tripolis, then, Peter got up and found us awake. After greeting us, he went out to the water basin to wash and pray, and we followed his example. After we had prayed together and sat down before him, he spoke about the need to keep pure. When it was now daylight, he allowed the crowds to enter. Once the crowd had come in, he greeted many of them as usual and began to speak:

lexical_decisions.chosen: water basin
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes a place or vessel supplying water, not necessarily a modern bathroom. Washing precedes prayer.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν περὶ τοῦ δεῖν ἁγνεύειν ἐποιεῖτο λόγον.
lexical_decisions.chosen: he spoke about the need to keep pure
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἁγνεύειν can concern ritual or moral purity; the discourse develops both and neither is excluded here.

passages.text: “Because of your great neglect of yourselves, your mind has sprouted the many harmful notions associated with religious worship, and you have become like land left uncultivated for lack of a farmer. You need much time for cleansing, so that your mind, receiving the true word imparted to you like good seed, may not choke it with evil thoughts and make it fruitless in the deeds that can save. Therefore those concerned for their own salvation must listen more continually, so that the wrongs multiplied over long periods may be brought into proportion, for cleansing, with the short time remaining through sustained .. effort. Since each person does not know the end of his own time, hurry to pull out the many thorns from your hearts, not little by little. For you will not be able to be cleansed that way, since you have lain uncultivated for so long.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς πολλὰς καὶ βλαβερὰς τῶν θρησκειῶν ὑπονοίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: the many harmful notions associated with religious worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains religious practices in the plural conceptual background; notions can also be suspicions or suppositions.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through sustained .. effort
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied edition has two consecutive dots after συνεχεῖ. Exactly two dots remain in the main text; unavailable content is not restored.

lexical_decisions.chosen: may be brought into proportion, for cleansing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The proportionality concerns accumulated errors and the short remaining time, with sustained effort as means; the wording is not replaced by a claim of automatic cleansing.

source_issues.issue: The supplied text contains exactly two dots between the adjective and noun. They remain as two dots in English; no unavailable wording is reconstructed.

passages.text: You will not otherwise endure undertaking the great effort needed for your cleansing unless you become angry with yourselves and rebuke yourselves for the ways in which, like useless servants, you were ambushed by agreeing with your evil desires. Then you will be able to apply your righteous anger to your mind like fire to a field left uncultivated. So if you do not have righteous fire—I mean anger against evil desires—learn what good things you have been ambushed and deprived of, what punishment you have been prepared for, and by whom you have been deceived. In this way your mind, becoming clear-minded and kindled to anger like fire by the teaching of the one who sent us, may be able to burn things away in opposition to desire. Believe me: if you are willing, you will be able to set everything right.

lexical_decisions.chosen: like useless servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses the POB servant gloss; the comparison retains the underlying bonded-status and master-accountability sense of δοῦλοι.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ.
lexical_decisions.chosen: may be able to burn things away in opposition to desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied genitive τῆς makes κατά naturally against, not according to. The rendering takes the phrase as expressing opposition in the consuming action and leaves τὰ as general things; it does not silently turn the genitive into an accusative or specify an unprinted object. Alternatively the phrase may be construed as the things directed against desire, though this sits awkwardly in the fire-and-anger argument.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ.
source_issues.issue: The genitive construction is awkward in the stated argument. The English preserves opposition to desire without changing the case or inventing a specific object; an alternative formal grouping is the things against desire. The consuming action itself is secure, but the phrase’s exact grouping is uncertain.

passages.text: You are an image of the invisible God. Therefore those who wish to practice reverence must not say that idols are an image of God and that they must therefore be revered. For the human being is God’s image. Whoever wishes to show reverence toward God does good to a human being, because the human body bears God’s image. But not everyone bears the likeness: that belongs to the pure mind of a good soul. Nevertheless, since we know that the human being was made “according to the image and according to the likeness” of God, we tell you to show reverence toward this human being, so that the gratitude may be credited to God, whose image he is. You must therefore offer honor to God’s image—that is, the human being—in this way: food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the unclothed, care to the sick, shelter to the stranger, and visits and whatever help is possible to the prisoner. Not to speak item by item: whatever good things someone wishes for himself, let him likewise provide for another who needs them. Then a good reward can be credited to him for having shown reverence toward God’s image. By the same reasoning, if he does not undertake to do these things, he will be punished for having neglected the image.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν δὲ ὁμοιότητα οὐκέτι πάντες, ἀλλὰ ἀγαθῆς ψυχῆς ὁ καθαρὸς νοῦς.
lexical_decisions.chosen: But not everyone bears the likeness: that belongs to the pure mind of a good soul.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the author’s image/likeness distinction rather than harmonizing them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα εἰς θεόν, οὗπέρ ἐστιν εἰκών, ἡ χάρις λογισθῇ.
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that the gratitude may be credited to God, whose image he is
lexical_decisions.rationale: χάρις can be gratitude, favor, or the benefit; gratitude is preferred in the transfer of honor to the one represented. The benefaction being reckoned as directed to God is another viable construal.

passages.text: What can it mean, then, to say that you revere every form for the sake of reverence toward God, when in every way you abuse the human being who truly is God’s image—murdering, committing adultery, stealing, and dishonoring him in many other ways? You ought not to do any evil that causes a person grief. But now you do everything that makes a person lose heart. For injustice and discouragement come through being murdered, having one’s property taken away, and all the other things you know you do not want to suffer. But you, deceived into evil by a certain malicious serpent through a notion of knowledge of many gods, show irreverence toward the true image—that is, the human being—while imagining that you show reverence toward insensible things.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a certain malicious serpent
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἑρπετόν is a creeping creature; serpent follows the recurring figure explicitly called ὄφις nearby without adding its identity as a name.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through a notion of knowledge of many gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the claim to knowledge and its many-gods qualification; it is not presented as the translator’s own true knowledge.

passages.text: Some say, “If he did not want them to exist, they would not exist, but would have been destroyed.” I too say that this certainly will happen when everyone has displayed his own choice toward him; then the present world will be changed. Yet even if you wanted him to act in this way, so that none of the things worshiped existed, tell us: which existing thing have you not worshiped? Do not some of you worship the sun, others the moon, others water, others earth, others mountains, others plants, others seeds, and others even a human being, as in Egypt? Then God would have had to leave nothing, not even us, so that there would be neither anything worshiped nor anyone worshiping. Truly, this is what the terrible serpent lurking within you wants to happen; he does not spare you. But it will not be so. For the thing worshiped commits no sin: it suffers violence at the hands of the person who wants to worship it. Even if all human beings judge unjustly, God does not. For it is not just for the one who suffers and the one who inflicts it to receive the same punishment—unless the former himself willingly accepts the honor belonging to the one who alone is most worthy of honor.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν αὐτῶν πρὸς αὐτὸν δείξωσιν προαίρεσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: has displayed his own choice toward him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains human choice and its orientation toward God without inserting a doctrine of predestination.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ αὐτὸς ἑκὼν ἀναδέξηται τὴν τοῦ μόνου τιμιωτάτου τιμήν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: unless the former himself willingly accepts the honor belonging to the one who alone is most worthy of honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The exception concerns a recipient of worship willingly accepting divine honor. No named example is added.

passages.text: “But,” someone says, “the worshipers themselves ought to be destroyed by the true God, so that no one else does this.” But you are not wiser than God, so as to offer him advice as someone more intelligent. He knows what he is doing. For he is patient with all who live in impiety, like a merciful father who loves humanity, knowing that even impious people become reverent. Many of the very people who revere shameful and insensible things have become clear-minded, stopped revering them and sinning, and taken refuge in the true God; through prayers and good deeds they have been saved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have become clear-minded
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses the POB clear-minded rendering for awakening from religious error, not an exclusively literal sobriety claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through prayers and good deeds they have been saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the author’s explicit linkage of salvation, prayers, and good deeds without imposing a denominational explanation.

passages.text: “But from the beginning he ought to have made us not even think about such things at all.” In saying this, you do not know what freedom of choice is or how it is possible to be truly good. For the person who is good by his own choice is truly good; the person made good by someone else’s compulsion is not truly so, because he is not what he is by his own choice. Since each person’s freedom produces what is truly good and reveals what is truly evil, God has arranged, through the circumstances, for becoming an enemy or a friend to lie within each person. “No,” someone says, “rather, he himself makes us think everything that we think.” Stop! What further blasphemy are you speaking when you say this? For if everything we think is put into effect in us by him, you are calling him the cause of sexual immoralities, shameless acts, greed, and every blasphemy. Stop speaking ill of him, you who ought to speak well of him and assign him every honor. And do not say, “God does not claim honor.” Even if he claims nothing, we still ought, with an eye to what is just, to repay with a thankful voice the one who has benefited us in every way.

lexical_decisions.chosen: freedom of choice
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally self-determination or being in one’s own power; the paragraph explicitly contrasts personal choice and external compulsion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through the circumstances
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑποθέσεις can denote situations, underlying conditions, or proposed matters; circumstances fits the arrangements in which choice operates without specifying their exact mechanism.

lexical_decisions.chosen: sexual immoralities, shameless acts, greed
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves distinct vice categories without embellishing sexual content or reducing all three to a generic evil.

passages.text: “But,” someone says, “we do better by thanking him and everyone else together.” In saying this, you do not know the plot against you. For suppose many physicians promise to treat one sick person but can do nothing, while one who really can heal does not administer his remedy, reasoning that if he heals the patient, others will take the credit. In the same way, when God is esteemed along with many who can do nothing, he does not bestow benefits. “What then?” someone says. “Is God indignant about this, if someone else gets the credit when he heals?” I say that even if he is not indignant, he still does not wish to become an accomplice in deception. For when he does good, the idol that has done nothing is also confirmed as having power. I too say that if the person infatuated with insensible things were not harmed in his nature, perhaps God would have put up even with this. So become clear-minded for the sake of salvation and think what is reasonable. For God, being without need, himself needs nothing and is not harmed. It is we who benefit or are harmed. Just as Caesar is neither harmed when he is reviled nor benefited when he is thanked, but safety belongs to the one who thanks him and destruction to the one who reviles him, so those who speak well of God do not benefit him at all but save themselves. Likewise, those who blaspheme do him no injury but are themselves destroyed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ μὴ φυσικῶς ἠδίκητο πρὸς ἀναίσθητα ἐπτοημένος, ἴσως ἂν καὶ τοῦτο ὑπομεμενήκει
lexical_decisions.chosen: if the person infatuated with insensible things were not harmed in his nature, perhaps God would have put up even with this
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject of being harmed and infatuated is understood as the worshiper, while the subject of putting up with this is God, who immediately afterward is explicitly said not to suffer harm. φυσικῶς can also mean naturally. The Greek leaves these subjects implicit, so this contextual subject differentiation is disclosed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Caesar
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the imperial name/title without identifying a particular emperor.

passages.text: “But,” someone says, “it is not the same with a human being and God.” I agree that it is not the same. For the punishment is greater for having shown irreverence toward one who is greater, and less for the one who has sinned against someone lesser. Thus, just as God is greater than all, the person who has shown irreverence toward him will undergo greater punishment for having sinned against someone greater. It is not that God retaliates with his own hand; rather, all creation is indignant at this and pursues the offender by its nature. For neither will the sun give the blasphemer light, nor the earth its fruits, nor a spring its water, nor the ruler established in Hades give the soul there rest, since even now, while the world’s allotted term still stands, all creation shares in the indignation. Therefore neither does heaven provide rain in full nor the earth its fruits, and most people are consequently brought to ruin. Even the air itself, inflamed with anger, changes to act as a pestilence. Yet whatever good things we enjoy, he compels creation by his mercy to act with love toward us. This is how all creation is angry with you who dishonor the maker of all.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἐν ᾅδῃ τῇ ψυχῇ ὁ ἐκεῖ καθεστὼς ἄρχων τὴν ἀνάπαυσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: nor the ruler established in Hades give the soul there rest
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains Hades as the source’s named realm; it is not replaced by a later, more specific doctrine of hell.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου προθεσμίας ὑφεστώσης
lexical_decisions.chosen: while the world’s allotted term still stands
lexical_decisions.rationale: The stated time-limit belongs to the world; the text does not supply its length.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ αὐτοῦ ἐλέῳ εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν φιλανθρωπίαν βιάζεται τὴν κτίσιν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: he compels creation by his mercy to act with love toward us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reflexive/possessive references are retained contextually: God compels creation toward humane treatment of us. The active force of βιάζεται is not softened into permission.

passages.text: For even if you escape punishment through the dissolution of the body, how will you be able through destruction to escape your soul, which is indestructible? For even the soul of the impious is immortal; it would have been better for them not to have it indestructible. Punished by unquenchable fire with unending punishment and not dying, it cannot come to an end, to its own hurt. But perhaps one of you will say, “You frighten us, Peter.” Then teach us how we are to state things as they are while remaining silent, for we cannot make them known to you otherwise. If we remain silent, you are ambushed by evils through ignorance; if we speak, we are suspected of frightening you on a false premise. How, then, are we to deal with the evil lurking within you and cunningly sowing notions hostile to God under the pretext of friendship with God? Be reconciled with yourselves: taking refuge in him with good deeds is for your salvation. There is within you an irrational desire hostile to God; through a pretension to intelligence, it strengthens ignorance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν κακῷ ἐνδομυχοῦντι
lexical_decisions.chosen: the evil lurking within you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The possessive phrase τὴν ὑμετέραν has no expressed feminine noun in the supplied wording. Within you preserves the contextual location of the lurking evil without inventing a named organ or restoring Greek words.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ κακῷ τῷ αὐτῆς τέλος λαβεῖν οὐκ ἔχει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: it cannot come to an end, to its own hurt
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains endless survival as harmful to the punished soul; the author’s claim is not harmonized with annihilation.

passages.text: Others say, “God has not cared about us.” This too is false. For if he truly did not care, he would not make his sun rise on good and evil people or send his rain on the righteous and unrighteous. Others say, “We are more reverent because we revere both him and the statues.” I do not think that someone who says this to a king—“I assign you the same honor as I do the dead and discarded dung”—will come off well. But someone will say, “Do you call our objects of reverence dung?” Yes, I say. For you made them useless to yourselves by counting them among objects of worship, although their substance might have served some other purpose, even the use of dung. But now it is not useful even for this, since you have reshaped it and worship it. How can you, the most impious of all, also claim to be more reverent? For this one incomparable sin alone you truly owe the destruction of your soul, if you persist. Just as a son who receives many benefits from his father and gives someone else, who is not his father, the honor owed to his father certainly becomes disinherited, so, when he lives according to his father’s judgment and gives thanks for the benefits, he reasonably becomes an heir.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῶν ἴσως εἰς ἄλλο τι (εἰς χρῆσιν κόπρου) εὐχρηστησάσης.
lexical_decisions.chosen: although their substance might have served some other purpose, even the use of dung
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the parenthetical comparison with useful dung rather than upgrading the idols into useful objects of worship.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταύτῃ αὐτῇ τῇ μιᾷ καὶ ἀσυγκρίτῳ ἀμαρτίᾳ ψυχῆς ὄλεθρον ὀφείλοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: For this one incomparable sin alone you truly owe the destruction of your soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the severe stated consequence, with the following if-you-persist condition retained in the main text.

passages.text: Others say, “We shall be acting impiously if we abandon the objects of reverence handed down to us from our fathers, for it is like keeping something entrusted to us.” By this reasoning, then, even if someone’s father is a robber or leads a shameful life, should the son not become clear-minded and choose what is better, lest he act impiously and sin by not doing the same things as his parents? How senseless are those who say, “We worship these things so as not to trouble him himself,” as though God were troubled by being praised but not troubled by being blasphemed through ingratitude! Why, then, when rain is withheld, do you all look toward heaven and offer prayers and entreaties? And when you succeed, why do you forget so quickly? For after reaping or gathering the vintage, you immediately assign the firstfruits to idols that are nothing, quickly forgetting the God who did you good. Then you go into sacred groves and temples and feast while performing sacrifices. For this reason some of you say, “These things have been well devised for comfort and feasting.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἂν λῃστοῦ τις ἢ πατρὸς ἢ αἰσχροβίου
lexical_decisions.chosen: even if someone’s father is a robber or leads a shameful life
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compressed phrase is construed in the father/son contrast that follows, with robber and shameful-living characterizing the father. It is not changed into a command to preserve immoral ancestral practices.

passages.text: Senseless people, become just judges of what is being said. For even if one ought to give oneself over to bodily enjoyment here, which feast is better: one by rivers and woods and groves, where there are banquets and drinking parties and shaded places, or one where there is the frenzy of demons, cutting of hands, cutting off of genitals, fits of fury and madness, clipping of hair, boasts, possession, shrieks, and all those things done theatrically to astound the senseless, so that you offer your owed prayers and thanksgivings to things deader even than the dead?

lexical_decisions.chosen: cutting of hands, cutting off of genitals
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both named ritual injuries soberly without euphemism or added detail.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to things deader even than the dead
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the pointed comparative and its rhetorical excess.

passages.text: And why do you do these things gladly? Since the serpent nesting within you, who sowed fruitless desire in you, does not want to tell you, I will remind you by explaining. It is like this: in the worship of God it is proclaimed that one must be clear-minded, exercise self-control, master anger, not appropriate what belongs to others, live justly, reasonably, steadily, and gently, and discipline oneself in deprivation rather than, when lacking something, take it unjustly from someone else and be filled. But among the so-called gods, the opposite happens. Some commands are also given to inspire awe at righteousness; yet even if you perform all the commands, ignorance of God alone is sufficient for your punishment. Nevertheless, you gather at the places you have assigned to them, gladly become drunk, and kindle altars. Their drifting sacrificial smoke, through its power, brings even the blind and deaf spirits to the place where they smell it. Thus, of those there, some are filled with possession, others with strange foods, while others turn to shameless conduct and others to thefts and murders. For the vapor of the blood there and the libation of wines set even the impure spirits themselves dancing. Lurking within you, they make you take pleasure in what goes on there, surround you through dreams with false visions, and punish you with countless afflictions. For under the pretext of the so-called sacrificial offerings you are filled with fierce demons, who also kill you while cunningly escaping your notice, so that you do not understand the plot against you. For under the pretext of some abuse, necessity, passion, anger, or grief, they remove you from life by hanging, by drowning you in water, by throwing you from a cliff, by your own hand, by a stroke, or by some other affliction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἔνια εἰς κατάπληξιν δικαιοσύνης παραγγέλλεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: Some commands are also given to inspire awe at righteousness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase relates certain commands to an impressive effect associated with righteousness. An impressive display of righteousness is another viable rendering; the main text does not decide that all such commands are merely fraudulent.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ κνίσα ῥεμβομένη καὶ τὰ τυφλὰ καὶ κωφὰ πνεύματα διὰ τῆς ἐξουσίας ἄγει εἰς τὸν τῆς ὀσφρήσεως αὐτῶν τόπον.
lexical_decisions.chosen: Their drifting sacrificial smoke, through its power, brings even the blind and deaf spirits to the place where they smell it.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the attributed power of sacrificial smoke and the smell-language concerning blind and deaf spirits, without substituting modern causal explanation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ αὐτὰ χοροῖ τὰ ἀκάθαρτα πνεύματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: set even the impure spirits themselves dancing
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the dancing image, not merely attraction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by your own hand, by a stroke
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains distinct claimed causes of death without adding clinical detail.

passages.text: But none of us can suffer anything of this kind. Rather, they are themselves punished by us when, after entering someone, they beg us to let them come out slowly. But perhaps someone will say, “Some who revere God also fall into such afflictions.” I say that this is impossible. For the God-revering person is the one I mean, the one who truly reveres God, not someone merely called so. The one who truly is such carries out the commands of the law given him. If someone acts impiously, he is not reverent. In the same way, if a foreigner practices the law, he is a Jew; a Jew who does not practice it is a Greek. For the person who believes God practices the law, and through this faith also removes the other afflictions that resemble mountains and weigh him down. But the person who does not practice the law plainly deserts his post because he does not believe God. Thus, as a sinner who is not a Jew, because of sin he is overpowered by the afflictions appointed to punish sinners. By God’s will, determined from the beginning, punishment justly follows those who revere him on account of their transgressions. This happens so that, after exacting the sin like a debt through torment, it may present those who have turned back clean at the judgment of all. For just as luxury here becomes for the wicked a loss of eternal good things, so punishments are sent to Jews who transgress as an exaction, so that, after receiving the due for their transgression here, they may be released from the eternal punishment there.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they beg us to let them come out slowly
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes us as the object of beg and demons as the implied subject of coming out. Permission is implicit. Beg us to withdraw slowly is another grammatical grouping, but the expulsion context favors the former.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a Jew who does not practice it is a Greek
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the author’s explicit Jew/Greek categories defined here through observance. Greek can function as Gentile in the religious argument; no literal change of ancestry is added.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who have turned back
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the turning verb distinct from μετανοέω/reorient.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as an exaction
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the debt-collection image of punishment.

passages.text: But you cannot say these things, for you do not believe that things there are as we say—I mean the place where everyone receives repayment. Therefore, ignorant of what benefits you, you are ambushed by temporary pleasures so as not to receive eternal things. We therefore try to demonstrate what benefits you, so that, fully assured about the promises of reverence toward God, through good actions you may be able to inherit with us the age without sorrow. Until you come to know us, then, do not be angry with us as though we were lying about the good things we want for you. For we have not begrudged bringing you what we consider true and good; on the contrary, we have been eager to make you fellow heirs of the good things we believe in. For this is how one must speak to unbelievers. But that we really speak truth about what we say you will not be able to know unless you first obey with a love of truth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: obey with a love of truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπακούω can be listen or obey; obey retains the demanded response while the adverb retains love of truth.

passages.text: For the present, therefore, even if the serpent lurking within you wishes to ambush you in countless ways, putting evil thoughts and distractions into you, you must contend against him all the more in this way: listen to us continually. For you who have been so greatly deceived must sit together and learn how to chant against him. Otherwise it is impossible. By chanting against him, I mean resisting his evil counsels with reason, remembering that from the beginning he brought death into the world through a promise of knowledge.

lexical_decisions.chosen: how to chant against him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the incantation metaphor that the author immediately defines as rational resistance, not a newly supplied magical formula.

passages.text: Therefore the prophet of truth, knowing that the world was greatly deceived and seeing that it had agreed with evil, did not love peace with it, since that peace arose from error. Setting out that it ultimately brings death upon all who agree with evil, in place of error he cast into those who had become clear-minded an anger against the one who had ambushed them, like fire and resembling a sword. Holding out the word, he does away with ignorance through knowledge, as though cutting and separating the living from the dead. So, as evil was overcome by knowledge in accordance with the law, war gripped everything. For the sake of salvation a son who yielded separated from a disobedient father, or a father from a child, or a mother from a daughter, or a daughter from a mother—in short, relatives from relatives and friends from companions.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅτι εἰς τέλος ἐπιφέρει πᾶσιν τοῖς πρὸς κακίαν ὁμογνωμονοῦσιν παραθεὶς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Setting out that it ultimately brings death upon all who agree with evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object brought is implicit. Death is inferred from the end of 11.18 and the ensuing living/dead contrast. The it can be the peace founded on error or its sustaining error; no new punishment is specified.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a son who yielded
lexical_decisions.rationale: The recipient of yielding is not explicit. The saving instruction is contextual, but the English does not insert that recipient.

source_issues.source_quote: ὅτι εἰς τέλος ἐπιφέρει πᾶσιν τοῖς πρὸς κακίαν ὁμογνωμονοῦσιν παραθεὶς
source_issues.issue: The object of brings upon is implicit. Death in the main text is inferred from the immediately preceding death-language and ensuing living/dead contrast. The antecedent can be error-based peace or its sustaining error.

passages.text: And let no one say, “How is this just, for parents to be separated from children and children from parents?” It is entirely just. For if by staying with them they not only did them no good but also perished with them, how is it not just for the one who wants to be saved to be separated from the one who does not want this but wishes them to perish together? Moreover, those who had understood what is better did not themselves want to be separated, but to remain with them and benefit them by teaching better things. Therefore the disobedient, unwilling to listen to them, themselves fought against them, separating from them, persecuting them, and hating them. But those who suffered these things pitied them as people ambushed by ignorance and, taught to understand, prayed for those who mistreated them, having learned that ignorance is the cause of sin. For the teacher himself, when nailed up, prayed to the Father that the sin of those killing him might be forgiven, saying, “Father, forgive them their sins, for they do not know what they are doing.” Becoming imitators of the teacher themselves, in their sufferings they prayed for those who inflicted them, as they had been taught. Thus they did not separate because they hated their parents, since they even offered prayers for those who were not their parents but had become enemies, and try to love them as they were commanded.

lexical_decisions.chosen: taught to understand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative connects instruction in understanding with the prayerful response, not with a newly supplied revelation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they ... separate
lexical_decisions.rationale: Bracketed letters are already supplied by the selected edition; no new restoration has been made.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who were not their parents
lexical_decisions.rationale: Follows the supplied bracketed reading and preserves the contrast with enemies.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when nailed up
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the physical nail-language.

passages.text: But tell me: how do you love your parents? If you do so with a constant regard for what is just, I join in your prayer; but if merely as it happens, I do not, for even on a small pretext you can become their enemies. If you love with knowledge, tell us what “parents” means. You will say, “Founders of a family line.” Why, then, have you not loved the origin of all things, if you have undertaken to do this with a just mind? But even now you will say, “We have not seen him.” Why, then, do you flatter insensible things without having searched? Even if it was difficult for you to know what God is, you could not fail to know what is not God, so that you might reason that God is not wood, not stone, not bronze, or anything else made of perishable matter.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the origin of all things
lexical_decisions.rationale: γένος links the argument to lineage and parentage. Origin or source here refers to God; progenitor of all is a viable more explicitly personal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I join in your prayer
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the prayer compound; join in wishing this is also possible, rather than bare agreement.

passages.text: Were they not shaped by iron—and was not the iron that shaped them softened by fire—and is not fire itself extinguished by water? Does not water get its motion from wind, and does not wind have the origin of its movement from the God who made all things? For this is what the prophet Moses said: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and God’s Spirit was borne over the water.” And when God speaks, this Spirit, like his hand, fashions everything, separating light from darkness and spreading out the visible heaven after the invisible one, so that the regions above may be inhabited by the angels of light, while those below may be administered by the human being together with all things made for his sake.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ δὲ ὕδωρ οὐχ ὑπὸ πνεύματος τὴν κίνησιν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: Does not water get its motion from wind
lexical_decisions.rationale: πνεῦμα can be wind or spirit. Wind fits the physical water-motion argument; the same word recurs as God’s Spirit in the quotation, preserving an important lexical link in these notes.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the origin of its movement
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here displacement or movement is intended, not religious ecstasy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ τὸν ἀόρατον οὐρανὸν τὸν φαινόμενον ἐφαπλῶσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: spreading out the visible heaven after the invisible one
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the visible/invisible distinction and after without supplying numbered heavens.

passages.text: For it was for you, the human being, that God commanded the water on the face of the earth to withdraw, so that the earth could offer you fruits. He made openings so that it might provide springs for you, streams of rivers might appear, and animals might be cast up. To put it briefly, so that everything could be at your service. Is it not for you that winds blow for the production of fruits, rains are brought, and seasonal turnings occur? Indeed, the sun and moon, together with the other stars, carry out their risings and settings for you, and rivers and lakes, together with all the springs, serve you. Therefore, just as greater honor was given to you, insensible though you are, so greater punishment through fire has been prepared for you in your ingratitude, because you were unwilling to know the one whom you ought to have known before all others.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He made openings
lexical_decisions.rationale: Bored holes or passages; no modern geological mechanism is specified.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and animals might be cast up
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the casting-up image, not generic creation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and seasonal turnings occur
lexical_decisions.rationale: The turnings can concern the sun or seasons; the broader cyclical wording is retained.

passages.text: Even now, recognize from the lesser things the cause of all things, reasoning that water produces all things, that water receives its coming into being through the movement of spirit, and that spirit has its origin from the God of all. This is how you ought to reason, so that through reason you may be able to reach God, recognize your lineage, be born again through first-born water, and become an heir of the parents who begot you for incorruptibility.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ δὲ ὕδωρ ὑπὸ πνεύματος κινήσεως τὴν γένεσιν λαμβάνει
lexical_decisions.chosen: water receives its coming into being through the movement of spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: πνεῦμα can also be wind, as in 11.22. Spirit emphasizes its divine origin and the rebirth argument; physical wind remains a material alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be born again through first-born water
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the unusual birth-wording. Primordial water is a contextual alternative but would conceal the explicit birth epithet.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν πρὸς ἀφθαρσίαν γεννησάντων σε γονέων
lexical_decisions.chosen: the parents who begot you for incorruptibility
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source has plural parents and does not identify them in this clause; neither a singular parent nor specific identities are substituted.

passages.text: Therefore come readily, like a son to a father, so that God may set down ignorance as the cause of your sins. But if, even after being called, you are unwilling or delay, you will perish by God’s just judgment, unwanted because you were unwilling. And do not imagine that if you become more reverent than all the reverent people who have ever existed, but remain unbaptized, you will ever be able to attain hope. For in this way you will rather undergo greater punishment, because you did not do good deeds in a good way. For doing good is good when it is done as God commanded. But if you are unwilling to be baptized as he determined, by serving your own will you are hostile to his purpose.

lexical_decisions.chosen: unwanted because you were unwilling
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the repeated will-wordplay and passive rejection; not being willed because you did not will is more formally literal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you did not do good deeds in a good way
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the distinction between good deeds and doing them well.

passages.text: But perhaps someone will say, “What does being baptized in water contribute to reverence?” First, you do what God determined. Second, being born again out of water to God, out of fear you exchange the first birth that came to you through desire, and thus you can attain salvation; otherwise it is impossible. For the prophet swore to us in this way, saying, “Truly I tell you, unless you are born again in living water, into the name of Father, Son, Holy Spirit, you will certainly not enter the kingdom of the heavens.” Therefore come. For there is something merciful there, borne upon the water from the beginning, .... those baptized with the thrice-blessed naming, and rescues them from the punishment to come, offering to God, as gifts, the good deeds of the baptized themselves from their baptism onward. Therefore take refuge in the water, for this alone can quench the onrush of fire. The person not yet willing to come to it still bears the spirit of madness, because of which he is unwilling to come to “living water” for his own salvation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αἰτίᾳ φόβου τὴν ἐξ ἐπιθυμίας πρώτην σοι γενομένην καταλλάσσεις γένεσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: out of fear you exchange the first birth that came to you through desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: Fear motivates the exchange; desire characterized the first birth. The replacement birth is the stated water-rebirth; physical birth is not explicitly labeled sinful.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐὰν μὴ ἀναγεννηθῆτε ὕδατι ζῶντι, εἰς ὄνομα πατρός, υἱοῦ, ἁγίου πνεύματος
lexical_decisions.chosen: unless you are born again in living water, into the name of Father, Son, Holy Spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: Follows this quotation’s wording, not the wording of a familiar canonical verse; no unprinted conjunctions are inserted into the name sequence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: borne upon the water from the beginning, .... those baptized
lexical_decisions.rationale: Exactly four printed gap dots remain. The missing predicate governing those baptized is not restored, leaving the English visibly interrupted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with the thrice-blessed naming
lexical_decisions.rationale: Naming or invocation associated with baptism, described as thrice-blessed; no later doctrinal explanation is added.

lexical_decisions.chosen: bears the spirit of madness
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the historical author’s spirit-language; λύσσα is raging madness, also rabid frenzy, not a supplied modern clinical diagnosis.

source_issues.issue: Exactly four printed dots mark unavailable wording. The governing predicate before those baptized is left interrupted; no reconstruction is supplied.

passages.text: Come, then, whether you are righteous or unrighteous. For if you are righteous, all you lacked was to be baptized for salvation. But if unrighteous, in addition to being baptized for the forgiveness of things done in ignorance, doing good remains for you in addition to baptism, in proportion to your impiety. Therefore, whether you are righteous or unrighteous, hurry to be born to God, for delay brings danger because the time appointed for death is unknown. Through doing good, show your likeness to the Father who begets you out of water, honoring the true God as Father as one who loves truth. Honor to him is for you to live as he, being righteous, wills; the will of the righteous is not to act unjustly. Injustice is murdering, committing adultery, hating, coveting, and things like these; and there are many forms of these.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ ἀναλογίαν τῆς ἀσεβείας ἡ ἐπὶ τὸ βάπτισμα εὐποιΐα
lexical_decisions.chosen: doing good remains for you in addition to baptism, in proportion to your impiety
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains proportional doing-good in addition to baptism, neither rewriting baptism as merely symbolic nor deleting the required deeds.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ἐξ ὕδατος γεννῶντί σε πατρί, διὰ τῆς εὐποιΐας τὴν ὁμοιότητα δείξας
lexical_decisions.chosen: Through doing good, show your likeness to the Father who begets you out of water
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves water-birth and likeness through conduct without supplying a further causal mechanism.

passages.text: Yet one must add to these something that does not concern dealings with human beings but belongs specifically to the worship of God. I mean keeping clean: not having intercourse with one’s own wife when she is menstruating, because God’s law commands this. What then? If keeping clean did not belong also to God’s worship, you would gladly roll about like beetles. Therefore, as human beings possessing something beyond the irrational animals—being rational—cleanse your heart of evils through heavenly reasoning, and wash your body with a bath. For keeping clean is truly good, not because bodily purity takes precedence over cleansing of the heart, but because cleanliness follows goodness. Our teacher even exposed some of the Pharisees and scribes among you as hypocrites, although they are set apart and, as scribes, know the laws better than others, because they purified only what is visible to people but neglected the pure things of the heart, visible to God alone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἐν ἀφέδρῳ οὔσῃ τῇ ἰδίᾳ γαμετῇ μὴ κοινωνεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: not having intercourse with one’s own wife when she is menstruating
lexical_decisions.rationale: Makes the euphemistic monthly-separation term intelligible without embellishment; this is the ancient author’s restriction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς οἱ κάνθαροι ἡδέως ἂν ἐκυλίεσθε
lexical_decisions.chosen: you would gladly roll about like beetles
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the comparison without supplying the substance in which the beetles roll.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐχ ὡς ὅτι προηγεῖται τῆς κατὰ τὴν καρδίαν κάθάρσεως ἡ τοῦ σώματος ἁγνεία
lexical_decisions.chosen: not because bodily purity takes precedence over cleansing of the heart
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the denial of bodily priority and the simultaneous affirmation of bodily cleanliness.

passages.text: So he truly used this express statement toward their hypocrites, not toward all of them. For he even said that some should be listened to, because they had been entrusted with Moses’ seat. But to the hypocrites he said, “Woe to you, hypocritical scribes and Pharisees, because you clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside it is full of filth. Blind Pharisee, first clean the inside of the cup and dish, so that their outsides too may become clean.” And this is true. For when the mind has been enlightened by knowledge, the person who has learned can be good, and becoming clean follows this. Good care for the outward body comes from the inward understanding. Just as inattention to the body cannot produce care for the mind, so the person who is clean inside can also clean the outside. But the one who cleans the outside does this with regard to people, looking toward praise, and with the praise of the onlookers has nothing before God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπό γε τῆς κατὰ τὸ σῶμα ἀναισθησίας τῆς διανοίας πρόνοια γενέσθαι οὐ δύναται
lexical_decisions.chosen: inattention to the body cannot produce care for the mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναισθησία can be lack of feeling, perception, or concern. Inattention is preferred in the care argument; bodily insensibility remains an alternative. The text is not changed to a word meaning washing or cleanliness.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἐπαίνῳ τῶν ἱστορούντων παρὰ τῷ θεῷ οὐδὲν ἔχει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: and with the praise of the onlookers has nothing before God
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the contrast between human praise and standing before God without adding a specified reward.

passages.text: Who does not see that it is better not to come together with a woman during her monthly condition, but after she has become clean and been immersed? And after intercourse one must also immerse oneself. If you shrink from doing this, recall how you pursued the parts of purity when you worshiped insensible idols. Be ashamed that here, where you ought to undertake not, I say, something greater, but simply the whole of purity, you become more reluctant. So consider the one who made you act there, and you will understand who it is that puts reluctance toward purity into you here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after she has become clean and been immersed
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this repeated purity setting βαπτίζω denotes bodily immersion; the same verb is baptized in the initiation setting. The contextual gloss difference does not claim different Greek words.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after intercourse one must also immerse oneself
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains repeated immersion after sexual intercourse, not mere inward purity or a newly asserted doctrine of repeated initiation.

passages.text: But one of you will say, “Must we then do whatever we did among idols?” I tell you: not everything, but whatever you did well, and here to a greater degree. For whatever is done well in error derives from the truth, just as if something is done badly in the truth, it comes from error. Therefore reclaim what is yours from everywhere, not what belongs to others, and do not say, “If those who have been deceived do something good, we ought not to do it.” For by this reasoning, if someone who reveres idols does not murder, we ought to murder because the person in error does not murder.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπολάβετε οὖν ὑμῶν πανταχόθεν τὰ ἴδια, μὴ τὰ ἀλλότρια
lexical_decisions.chosen: Therefore reclaim what is yours from everywhere, not what belongs to others
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the ownership/reclamation metaphor, not a blanket rejection of practices also found outside the community.

passages.text: No: rather, do more, so that if those in error do not murder, we do not even become angry; if the person in error does not commit adultery, we do not even think of it in the first place; if the person in error loves the one who loves him, we also love those who hate us; if the person in error lends to those who have, we also lend to those who do not have. In short, we who hope to inherit the boundless age ought to do better than the good things done by those who know only the present age. We know that if their deeds, examined alongside our deeds on the day of judgment, are found equal in doing good, we too must be put to shame, while they, through error having done what is against them, must perish. I spoke of being put to shame in this respect: we did not do more than those of whom we also knew more. But if we are to be put to shame for displaying good deeds equal to theirs and not more, how much more if we display less good conduct than theirs?

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ τὸν ἄπειρον αἰῶνα ἐλπίζοντες κληρονομεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: we who hope to inherit the boundless age
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄπειρος means boundless or endless; αἰών remains age, contrasting the present age.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those of whom we also knew more
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative expresses greater knowledge and responsibility; knew more than they did is an alternative English expansion.

passages.text: That on the day of judgment the actions of those who have known the truth are indeed measured against the good deeds of those who have been deceived, the one who does not lie himself taught us ...., saying to those who neglected to come and listen to him, “The queen of the south will rise with this generation and condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom; and look, something greater than Solomon is here, and you do not believe.” To those among the people who were unwilling to reorient at his proclamation, he said, “Men of Nineveh will rise with this generation and condemn it, because on hearing they reoriented in response to Jonah’s proclamation; and look, something greater ... is here, and no one believes.” Thus, setting over against each of their acts of impiety those from the nations who had acted, to condemn those in reverence toward God who had not done even as much good as those who had been deceived, he admonished those with understanding not merely to do good things equally with the nations, but to do more. My discourse flowed on, taking its starting point from the need to observe the menstrual period and to immerse oneself after intercourse: not to reject such purity even if those who have been deceived practice it, since those in error who do good serve to condemn those in reverence toward God, although they themselves are not saved. For their honoring of purity is because of error, not because of worship of the true Father and God of all.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who does not lie himself taught us ....
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected edition has four gap dots; exactly four remain, without reconstruction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and look, something greater ... is here
lexical_decisions.rationale: Exactly three gap dots remain. No familiar proper name from another witness is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they reoriented in response to Jonah’s proclamation
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses POB reorientation terminology, traditionally repented, preserving the stated occasion of the response.

lexical_decisions.chosen: although they themselves are not saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the author’s explicit non-salvation claim about people in error who nonetheless do good.

source_issues.issue: Exactly 4 printed gap dots remain in the English; no unavailable words are restored.
Exactly 3 printed gap dots remain in the English; no unavailable words are restored.

passages.text: After saying this, he dismissed the crowds and, as usual, shared salt with his closest friends and rested. By acting and discoursing in this way, on each occasion he brought people securely to God’s law, exposing the supposed ones along with the supposed destiny, and showing that there is no spontaneity, but the world is governed according to providence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: shared salt with his closest friends
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains salt-sharing rather than merely an unspecified meal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς νομιζομένους μετὰ τῆς νομιζομένης γενέσεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: the supposed ones along with the supposed destiny
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine plural has no expressed noun, contextually the supposed gods. γένεσις can be birth or natal destiny; destiny fits the contrast with providence, with natal fate or horoscope as more specific alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: there is no spontaneity
lexical_decisions.rationale: Spontaneous or chance occurrence; chance is a viable more idiomatic alternative.

passages.text: When three months had been completed, he instructed me to fast for days, led me to the nearby springs in the sea, and baptized me in water as ever-flowing water. After our brothers had thus feasted at my God-given rebirth, not many days later he turned to the elders before the whole assembly and gave these instructions: “Our Lord and prophet, who sent us, explained to us how the evil one conversed with him for forty days and, having gained no power against him, promised to send apostles from among his own subjects to deceive. Therefore, above all, remember not to ... an apostle or teacher or prophet before he has compared his proclamation with James, who is called the brother of my Lord and has been entrusted in Jerusalem with administering the assembly of the Hebrews, and has come to you with witnesses. This is so that the evil that conversed with the Lord for forty days and gained no power, and afterward fell like lightning from heaven to earth, may not send out a herald against you, as it has now put Simon in our way, proclaiming in the name of your Lord under the pretext of truth, but sowing error. For this reason the one who sent us said, ‘Many will come to me in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves; recognize them by their fruits.’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: he instructed me to fast for days
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied wording gives days but no explicit number; none is restored.

lexical_decisions.chosen: baptized me in water as ever-flowing water
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves ὡς and the ever-flowing quality instead of dropping the qualification.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ πρότερον . . . ἀντιβάλλοντα αὐτοῦ τὸ κήρυγμα Ἰακώβῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: not to ... an apostle or teacher or prophet before he has compared his proclamation with James
lexical_decisions.rationale: Exactly three dots remain. The governing action is unavailable and is not supplied as receive or trust. The negative/before relation, comparison of proclamation, and subsequent witnesses remain.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the brother of my Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps my here and your Lord later rather than harmonizing pronouns.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολλοὶ ἐλεύσονται πρὸς μὲ ἐν ἐνδύματι προβάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: Many will come to me in sheep’s clothing
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the supplied to me, rather than importing a familiar to you from another witness.

source_issues.issue: The three-dot gap leaves the governing action unavailable. Exactly three dots remain, with the negative, temporal relation, proclamation comparison and witnesses preserved rather than reconstruction from another witness.

passages.text: After saying these things, he sent the advance party to Antioch in Syria, telling them to wait there the following day. After they had gone, Peter drove away diseases, afflictions, and demons from large crowds who had been persuaded, baptized them in the nearby springs in the sea, and broke the Eucharist. He appointed Maron, who had received him and was by now mature, as overseer, designated twelve elders, appointed attendants, and organized arrangements for widows. He discussed the order that served the common or beneficial interest of the assembly and advised them to obey Maron the overseer. Since three months had now been completed, he took leave of those in Tripolis in Phoenicia and set out on the road to Antioch in Syria, with everyone accompanying us on our way with the appropriate honor.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to wait there the following day
lexical_decisions.rationale: The following is understood with the ordinary elliptical day; no exact date is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: broke the Eucharist
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source combines breaking with Eucharist/thanksgiving, implicitly its bread. The breaking action is retained rather than merely offered thanks.

lexical_decisions.chosen: overseer
lexical_decisions.rationale: Translates the office’s sense; bishop is the conventional title alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ διακόνους δείξας καὶ χηρικὰ συστησάμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: appointed attendants, and organized arrangements for widows
lexical_decisions.rationale: διάκονοι can be attendants or deacons. χηρικά means matters/institutions for widows, not an invented beneficiary list.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπέρ τε τοῦ κοινοῦ ἢ συμφέροντος τῆς ἐκκλησίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: that served the common or beneficial interest of the assembly
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the supplied or instead of silently changing it to and; the precise relation between common and beneficial remains loose.
